utterances.text: My question to you was: What did you do after the operation? Were those maps handed over to -- in the inner control branch or some other department, or were they discarded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The topographic map distributed to the commanders for further advancement in that direction were -- was not a document as such. The only document that could be -- would be preserved was the plan of attack with specific tasks. I'm not sure whether those maps were then sent to the headquarters. I believe the employees kept them on them, and it was of no use subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, may I just in order to avoid that other people find puzzles in our transcripts. Page 50, line 19, I take it that you wanted to refer to P1151 rather than P1051.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to move to page -- we are still on the same transcript. Mr. Turkalj, that is section 2. We were reading off page 15. If you could move to page 21. Mr. Turkalj, I'm asking you to move to your transcript which is on your desk. Page 21. I'm sorry, I think you're looking at -- it's a wrong one. Tab 2. Tab 3, sorry, the second section. Just below tab 3, yeah. This is regarding your -- the advance into Donji Lapac. This is what you say: "And again had you been supplied with the locations of potential enemy positions or facilities?" And if you could go to page 22. You say: "No, there was no particular intelligence. There was only the information that Lapac was a place which had rather strong forces." Now you entered Donji Lapac on the 7th of August, did you not, Mr. Turkalj, the special police forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I believe it to be the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you, in fact, entered -- or when the special police forces entered Donji Lapac, were there any enemy forces still present in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no fighting in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say there were no fighting in Donji Lapac, did you order artillery attacks on Donji Lapac before the forces entered?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: We did not open fire on Donji Lapac. Our artillery targeted the mountainous terrain in front of Donji Lapac. However, we did not target Donji Lapac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to page 32 on the same transcript, Mr. Turkalj. And there you say, the question is asked: "Am I right in saying that you as the commander of the artillery did not authorise shelling or use of artillery on Donji Lapac?" You say: "When Donji Lapac is regarded, we were acting targets that were in the front of our units. When the units practical entered Lapac, then Drazan Curkovic called with a request that the staff Markac, Sacic, or someone should contact the military and inform them about it, as military was acting with the artillery on Donji Lapac. It was within their authority and military authority." Your testimony was, and you elaborate this further, that when you, the special police forces entered Donji Lapac, HV forces were still shelling the town, and you had to, in fact, ask for a request to cease that fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by way of clarity, if the Prosecution can ask which Military District this firing into Donji Lapac was coming from, was it the Gospic Military District or the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is it Gospic, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask about the districts. I'm going to ask him about a completely different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the spirit of clarity, Mr. President, I thought I would raise that issue, that it is not the Split Military District firing into the Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, we know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to make a distinction which is apparently not relevant for Ms. Mahindaratne's question. If it would turn out to be relevant for the witness to make that distinction, he certainly will do so. Ms. Mahindaratne, perhaps you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Turkalj, now, you said the special police forces did not fire on Donji Lapac, or you did not order because there was no fighting there. So what was the HV artillery acting on in Donji Lapac when the special police forces entered there. What were they firing against?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is another question. Ms. Mahindaratne, I would not mind if you put another question. But let's try to first seek an answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- Mr. Turkalj, when your special police forces entered Donji Lapac, were HV forces still shelling the town, and is it true that you had to ask for -- that you requested to cease that fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is completely correct. The special police forces had entered Lapac, and at the outskirts of Lapac, it was the HV artillery that began opening fire from the direction of Udbina. Clearly, that artillery had links with the Military District of Gospic, given the fact that, at that point in time, they had no information on the pace of advancement of the special police, because Donji Lapac, I suppose, was along their axis or direction of attack. And as for the targets they were trying to engage, I can't tell you about that. It is also true that Mr. Curkovic used radio communication to find out from me whether it was us who was opening fire, and then they used communications to advise the Military District of Gospic that the police forces had already entered Lapac and that they should cease fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at your statement of 2004, Mr. Turkalj. That is it under tab 1 on your binder. Mr. Turkalj, the binder that is on your table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Paragraph 37, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 37, starting with third line you say this: "We did not target Donji Lapac with our artillery, but the military did. They were supposed to have reached Donji Lapac from Udbina before us, but they did not arrive. In fact, the army was still shelling the town, and we had to communicate with the army to tell team that they were in the town and to stop shelling it." Now, when you entered into the Donji Lapac town, you already said there was no fighting, there were no forces. Did you observe as to where the shells had impacted and where they were -- what they were shelling at in the town?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The statement is general when it comes to the shelling of the town. I don't know which targets they engaged. I didn't observe that, because I was not in Donji Lapac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have document 65 ter number 6172, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while that document is coming up, Mr. Turkalj, could you look at -- on this same statement, paragraph 69. And this is what you say, if I could read it to you, you say that: "Disciplinary matters were dealt with the special police, by the inner control department of the special police. Every unit had at least one member who worked for the inner control department, and sometimes even the commander of that unit did not know who that person was. The inner control dealt with all levels of discipline within the special police. All such matters would be reported to Mladen Markac, and he would decide how a member of the special police who committed a disciplinary offence would be dealt with. Crimes committed by a member of the special police would be handed to the criminal police by Mr. Markac, to be investigated. I am not aware of any criminal investigations that were undertaken by the criminal police into the special police, although I am sure that there were some criminal investigations into the members of the special police but not contacted with war activities." Now, if I could ask you to look at the document on your screen, Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Mahindaratne, for interrupting, but I would like you to have in mind the corrections that the witness made yesterday as regards to the inner control unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He didn't make any changes. He provided for the clarifications, which is on the record, so I did not read anything incorrectly, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I'd like you to look at the document on the screen. This is a proposal by -- issued by Mr. Mladen Markac regarding disciplinary measures to be taken against a member of the Lucko Unit, and it refers to the regulations he is acting under. Now, are you familiar with this matter? Because it -- at the end, it, in fact, refers to a report made by you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: This is correct. The only thing I can add is that within the Ministry of Interior, there was such a disciplinary procedure that for minor breaches of discipline every commander of a unit was duty-bound to pass a decision for a disciplinary procedure and for a major breach of discipline, it was prescribed that the proposal for initiating a procedure, Mr. Markac would issue. In other words, the commander of the special police. Every commander within the sector of the special police was duty-bound to provide information and documents based on which a proposal for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure may be drafted. In this particular instance, we can see that there is an Official Note of the head within the intervention unit of Lucko, and on the basis of this Mr. Markac, as assistant minister, produced a proposal for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In such instances where they were major disciplinary measures involved, was it always the case that you would submit the information to Mr. Markac in writing, you or the particular unit commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Within the sector of the special police, there was the practice in place whereby the chief or the commander would write everything and sent the proposal, and Mr. Markac would sign it. That was the practice. However, Mr. Markac could not submit a proposal for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure if he did not have from the unit the information and the task to -- or, rather, not the task, the request to initiate such a disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P1155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1155 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Turkalj, if I could ask you to look at your transcripts again. And that is the section under tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you could assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could look at page 52, this is section 1, for the record, P1150. Page 52. You're referring to disciplinary measures here, Mr. Turkalj, and you use specific examples. You say: "For example, there was one occasion the information sent by the inner control that a certain commander in [indiscernible], pardon my pronunciation, was cooperating with a certain firm or company involved in some criminal actions. And, for example, just if I were in a car given for my use, if I exaggerated the use of the car for not professional task, and sort of -- also the information could have been given to the General so that he could then make his own assessment based on such intelligence." Whom do you -- first of all, whom do you refer to there as General?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: In the interview, this was one of the general examples illustrating how the system functioned. It was only natural for me that if Mr. Markac had information to the effect -- a piece of information to the effect that I was using an official vehicle for private purposes, that was something that he would inquire about, and I don't see that there's anything stated here outside of what I have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was -- I wasn't criticising you for that. Mr. Turkalj, my question was -- just simply the first one was whom you referred to as General Markac. And the second question is do you know whether there was regular interaction between inner control branch and Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The internal control department was the component part of the sector of the special police. What sort of internal communication there was is something I cannot give you an answer to. The internal control department was part and parcel of the special police sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your interview you informed the investigators that you believe Mr. Markac driver was in the inner control branch. Were you referring to Mr. Anto Soljic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't know if I referred to Mr. Soljic, but Mr. Solic was the chief of the internal control department.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph that I read to you earlier from your statement, you referred to criminal matters committed by special police, and you said -- the part that I read was crimes committed by a member of the special police would be handed to the criminal police by Mr. Markac. I read it to you earlier on. Now, in the case of crimes committed by members of the special police, would a unit commander of a unit of a special police inform Mr. Markac of that particular members' deeds by way of a written report as in the case of disciplinary measures that we referred to earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I think that these are matters that are quite separate, one from the other. If we are talking about a criminal offence perpetrated by any member of the special police, the same sort of legislation applied to that individual as to every other citizens of the Republic of Croatia. As far as the workings of it were concerned, every member --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: -- if he learned that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, let me -- so I am very clear. Let me take you back to your statement to the part that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph 69 of your statement of 2004, and the English version, I'm reading five lines from the bottom of that paragraph. You say: "Crimes committed by a member of the special police would be handed to the criminal police by Mr. Markac to be investigated." Now how would -- if you as the commander of the Lucko Unit got information that a member of your unit had committed a crime -- now, your testimony is that it would be Mr. Markac who would hand him over to the crime police for investigation. How would you as the unit commander report that fact to Mr. Markac? How would you convey such information to Mr. Markac? Was it through a written report, as in the case of major disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. There are words thrown into the question that don't exist like major disciplinary measures. There was only disciplinary measures, then there is a difference between what a major disciplinary measure is and what a criminal act is. And I think those things need to be defined. Those are very important terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I referred exactly to the testimony. The witness referred to minor disciplinary measures and major, and he said in the case of major disciplinary measures, it was Mr. Markac who dealt with the proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are using the language that the witness used in his statements this is a reason to deny the objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement says in paragraph 69 "... would decide how a member of the special police who committed a disciplinary offence would be dealt with," not a major disciplinary offence, not a minor disciplinary offence. It is very specific in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I'm referring to his testimony previously. Let me read that part for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If could you give us, in order to avoid further confusion, the date --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just today's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today's evidence, page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Give me minute, Mr. President. Page 57, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness: "This is correct. The only thing I can add is that within the Ministry of Interior, there was such a disciplinary procedure that for minor breaches of discipline, every commander of a unit was duty-bound to pass a decision for a disciplinary procedure. And for a major breach of discipline, it was described that the proposal for initiating a procedure, Mr. Markac would issue."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're both a bit right. Minor and major appears. Although you're talking about measures major measures, which is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Proceed, yes, Mr. President, maybe I used the correct term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Perhaps repeat the question [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Turkalj, now in the case of a crime, how would you report that to Mr. Markac so that Mr. Markac could inform the crime police or hand over the perpetrator to crime police? Was that done by way of a written report as you -- you described earlier where we saw a document where you had tendered written reports, or would you do it verbally? What was the procedure set up for you to inform him of crimes committed by members of the special police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, Your Honour, just for a second. I would like Ms. Mahindaratne to clarify whether he is dealing with a known perpetrator or unknown perpetrator of the alleged crime. That is the [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think I was -- have I been referring to the question so clearly, I was referring to if a unit commander receives information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may ask that question. I mean, again, if such a distinction becomes relevant, then the witness will have to face it when answering that question, and then it will emerge anyhow. May I again urge the parties to not unnecessarily disrupt the flow of evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, let me repeat that question to you again. If you, as the commander of the Lucko Unit, receives informs that a member of the -- of your unit, Lucko Unit, had committed a crime, how would you inform that fact to the commander of the special police, Mr. Markac, so that he could take action to hand over that perpetrator to the crime police? Would you do that in writing, or would do you that verbally? I'm asking you to tell the Trial Chamber what the procedure is.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Your question is, in my view, a hypothetical one and that is how I'm going to answer it. It is definitely not the same if we know the perpetrator of a crime or not. It really matters. And I answered before -- or, rather, this part of your question in what way would I react as a commander, this is again down to the way in which the Ministry of the Interior works, and its rules have set out in detail in what way the police shall work or behave, where a report has been received of a criminal offence that was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, if a member of a special police unit, let's say you knew that one of your unit members had commented a crime, whether you know the identity of the perpetrator, you know the crime, and you have to have him investigated through crime police. Now, your testimony is that it would be Mr. Markac who would hand over that perpetrator to crime police. My question is simple. How would you bring that information that one of your members, whom you know the identity of, had committed a crime to Mr. Markac's knowledge? I think the question is very simple.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: The question is simple, but I believe my answer was too. If I knew of an individual having committed a crime as an authorised person, as a person working within the system, I would be duty-bound to report that to my superior, of course, and to the crime police, in order to -- for an investigation to be launched. If I know that the crime was committed. This is the duty of every member of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was focussing, how you would report. Would you write a report and send it, would you give a phone call to your superior, would you -- that's, I think, what Ms. Mahindaratne is interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, where a report was received of the -- of a crime having been committed, information has to be -- that information has to be reported to someone in -- verbally and, if necessary, in writing too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, I'm moving on to the event in Grubori. Your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we still have no clear answer. In your statement you say: "All such matters would be reported to Mladen Markac, and he would decide how a member of the special police who committed a disciplinary offence would be dealt with. Crimes committed by a member of the special police would be handed to the criminal police by Mr. Markac to be investigated." Now you say it should be reported to someone verbally or, if necessary, in writing too. What Ms. Mahindaratne would like to know, and I would like also like to know, in case of a crime, how would you report to Mr. Markac so that he could decide how to deal with the matter and how the known perpetrator would be handed over to the criminal police. Could you tell us in what cases would an oral report do or was, in cases of crimes, a written report to Mr. Markac always the appropriate way of reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot quite answer that. I don't know if it's been specifically said whether the report should be passed on verbally or in writing, the information of a criminal offence. Such information can be conveyed verbally and in writing. I would definitely convey that information in writing if I had learnt that some members of the special police committed something like that, and I would submit that to my superior. I believe that's what I said. I also said, however, that it would be the duty of every member of the Ministry of the Interior to inform the competent police branch where a criminal offence needs to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I'm -- I would like to take you to your testimony about the event in Grubori. Now, your testimony so far that some days after the incident Mr. Zeljko Sacic, the chief of the sector, ordered you to visit Gracac, and you did so, and then from there you went to Grubori with Mr. Celic and Balunovic. At which time Mr. Sacic, Janic, and Mr. Cermak, and a journalist by the name of Nada Zuriak [phoen] were present among others in Grubori. For the record, this evidence is in V000-5304, that's section 2, page 113 to 121.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, can I have ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter your testimony was that after the visit to Grubori, you went to Mr. Cermak's office in Knin in a convoy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I was advised by my colleagues who are listening to the Croatian translation that name of Mr. Markac was mentioned as one of the persons who visited Grubori, although this is not in the transcript, as I can see, but just for the record that there was Croatian translation of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think that was a mistake. I didn't mention Mr. Markac's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it was a mistake or something went missing or was changed. Yes, that is an incomplete part of the transcript at this moment, but special attention will be paid to it and it's clear, Ms. Mahindaratne, that you did not refer or at least did not intend to refer to Mr. Markac in this context. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document 3527, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, were you interviewed by the Ministry of Interior in 2004 about what you knew of Grubori, the incident in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: A colleague from the Ministry of the Interior interviewed me about the events in the area of Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the time that you were interviewed, did you take down notes of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I was not taking any notes, and I don't think the colleague was either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So that I don't waste time, Mr. Turkalj, with the permission of Court Mr. President if I could have the -- this particular document handed over to the witness during the break so that he could exam it without going through it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was also my intention to propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good. Mr. Turkalj, this Official Note, the original one, will be given to you. Would you please be so kind to read it during the next break and upon return to give any comments you may have on this Official Note of the interview that was held with you. I see you're nodding yes. I take that for a positive answer. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I'd like to you look at your transcripts. That is, V000-05305. That is section 3 of the transcript, for the record P1152. Madam Usher, if I could have your assistance. It's the last section under tab 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also in order to avoid puzzles for those who are reading transcripts later, I see on page 67, line 18, it reads document 3527. I was informed that it should be 2537. I don't know where the mistake comes from, but if you would agree, then it's now on the record, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go to page 20, and this is where you refer to -- on your return from Grubori to Knin to Mr. Cermak 's office, you talk about a conversation between Mr. Cermak -- Cermak and Sacic. This is what you say: "We were quite a number of people there, and talking there, but after some time I went out, and I was standing in a corridor with one special police member from Rijeka, I can confirm it. I don't recall how long it lasted." You're referring to the discussion between Mr. Sacic and Cermak. "From all of it, I still have one sentence in my head, when Cermak addressed Sacic and said words to the effect, Well, what have you done there?" That is what that you say: "It was something like a question, like an expression of anger. It's hard to comment now on what it really meant?" Now, were you aware as to why Mr. Cermak seemed displeased or angry at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: In my statement, I clearly said that other issues were discussed as well, while we were having coffee. As for this part of the statement of the transcript, it states that I did not hear exactly what the discussion was about and what was the manner of discussion. It was not an official meeting. In any case, I tried to tell as best I could as to what happened there. I believe Mr. Cermak asked what had taken place there because neither he nor anyone else knew at that point in time what did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go on to page -- on the same section, page 42. If you could turn down to page 42, Mr. Turkalj. And you further elaborate on that conversation. This is what you say: "But it is certain that Mr. Sacic said that one should say that there came to some combat activities and that some civilians got killed." Then a few lines down, you say: "It is certain that he said there: That it came to a conflict, and that within the conflict, those civilians were killed, conflict with some terrorists and than it should be said that way." If you go on to the next page, page 43. This is actually something that you said, but it is in the English, you know, translation it is recorded as if R.C., Robert Casey is saying, but this really the translation of the witness's statement. You say: "Sacic did not say that to me. I assume he said that to Cermak. So it wasn't -- I wasn't able to make any decisions about it." You were asked this question: "Is this a conversation you overheard though? "Yes, I heard that conversation and also later on in conversation with Celic --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that we cannot see what the witness said on the transcript; we see only the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think we can go to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I think the interprets can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's now on line 1, we see what was said by the witness in his own language. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the witness take his headphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, could you take your headphones off for a second. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm requesting that the counsel for the Prosecution put this extremely carefully to the witness. If you look at the transcript for this particular part of the interview, it is not as clear as Ms. Mahindaratne is actually putting it to the witness, and I can give you page references. If you go to page 42 of the transcript, you will see that what the witness actually says is, "Sacic said it is certain that one should say that there came to some combat activities and that some civilians got killed." Subsequently on page 45 in this interview, the witness says he assumes, he assumes that Sacic told Cermak. Not that he knows, not that he heard. And then you will find that the investigator then goes on and basically puts it to the witness on page 49 when Sacic was saying to Cermak was he suggesting that this was going to be the line, the party line, they got killed because they were terrorist there. We could spend a very long time on this, Your Honour, and I don't wasn't to waste the time or interrupt the flow of evidence, but I think if it is it read carefully, and if it's put honesty, frankly, the witness does not say that he overheard this conversation between Mr. Sacic and Mr. Cermak. He assumes it, and then the investigator take that assumption and puts it is to him as a fact. This is it your interpretation of the transcript in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm careful about interpretations. I'm reading what I see and how the questions were put, and I think it is not fair, frankly, to put it to this witness that he overheard this conversation because that is not what he said. And there are certainly leaps in logic that occur in this interview which do not really represent or go about in a way that actually seeks the truth. That is it the point I'm making here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would wait for a second so that you can respond both to Mr. Cayley's observations and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Kuzmanovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to further add, Your Honour, along those same lines as Mr. Cayley has stated, if you look at page 57 of the transcript, you can see where this is going. Because the investigator is essentially saying here and testifying basically advising Mr. Turkalj to be very very careful with your answers here because, as I said before, it is my intention, meaning the investigator, to get the Croatian courts to deal with certain members of Lucko Unit. And I'll make it clear now that I believe, and this is the investigator speaking, that Mr. Sacic in his position of rank has used that position to perhaps exert pressures on certain members of the Lucko Unit and -- let me go on to page 57. To support his, and I believe it's his proposal, to cover up the crimes by saying there were terrorists there. So this is the context in which these questions are being asked, not to elicit information as an investigator from this witness, but to basically pressure him, put words in his mouth, and put his case to the witness, and I think that's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is partially argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but I think the context in which you need to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have admitted this document into evidence, which allows us to clearly follow in every detail what the witness said, in response to what questions, how his statement developed, and please be assured that the Chamber has read, and the Chamber usually does not leave Grubori to the very end, if there's any time left. But sometimes we even start with certain portions to focus on -- at least I'm now speaking for myself. At the same time, Ms. Mahindaratne, you wanted to respond. Let me first give an opportunity for you to respond because you said it might save time, and I'm very much interested in --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, all this could have been simply avoided if the counsel just waited to hear my question. I was going to read back the transcript to the witness, and I was going to ask him to clearly state to Court what he heard in the course of that discussion. I wasn't going do anything unfair, in fairness to the witness and in fairness to everybody, that was going to be my question, and I think all this could have been prevented if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would say you would not add the kind of things the investigator added when he did put the questions to the witness at that time, which I would not have taught him if I ever would have given a course of examination of potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware of what may follow if you would unfairly put matters to the witness, that's clear now by the submissions made by the other parties, and you will have that in your mind when you put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, at the same time, perhaps before we continue, perhaps it would be better to have a break because it might take some time, I take it, the issue you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I'm going to read back to you because there was some interruptions, this is what you say. First let me read back to you what you said in your interview. "But it is certain that Mr. Sacic said that one should say that there came to some combat activities and that some civilians got killed. It is certain that he said there, and it came to a conflict, and that within the conflict those civilians were killed, conflict with some terrorists and that it should be said that way?" "Sacic did not say that to me. I assume he said that to Cermak, so it wasn't -- I wasn't able to make any decisions about it." "Yes, I heard that you -- is that a conversation you overheard, though?" "Yes, I heard that conversation, and also later on in conversation with Celic, Celic, Celic told me that Sacic told him that when writing report, it should be put that way." "When you spoke to Mr. Celic in Grubori did he at that time indicate to that you he had been told that he had got to put this in his report?" "No, I think afterwards. I don't know if we were talking about it then." And if you could go on to next page, page 44. "I think it was later on. Maybe it was only within the last year in those conversations that he mentioned that." Mr. Turkalj, I'm referring to page 44. And if you could move to page 45, you were asked a question again: "I appreciate that so what I want to do is go back. I just want to confirm what, what you heard Mr. Sacic say to Cermak about it being as a result of -- or suggesting it was a result of a conflict with terrorists. Can you just tell me exactly to the best of your recollection what was said?" "I have to say that I really cannot be certain how precisely it was said. More or less it was said that the special police without mentioning any unit, just in general, special police came across some terrorists there, and in their fighting some civilians got killed." Page 46: "Was he suggesting this was the story to be used or this was what his information was?" You were asked the question: "Who?" "When Sacic was saying this to Cermak, was he suggesting that this was going to be the line, the party line, they got killed because there were terrorists there?" "Yes, in that sense." "So I just wanted to make sure I got this right. Sacic was basically saying that this is the story we are going to use whether it was true or not." "Yes, that's what it would turn out to be." "Well, you say that's what it turned out to be. Is that what you understood it to mean at that time?" Page 47: "It is how I understood that, but I cannot repeat the exact words." "No, but ... but that was the ... the line that Mr. Sacic was going to do down, that however they were killed, it was as a result of terrorists being there." "Yes." "Whethers that with an a true story or not?" "Yeah, well, regardless of that."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, my question -- so that there is no room whatsoever for confusion, can you tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So that, Mr. Turkalj, now what I like you to do so there is no room whatsoever for confusion, can you tell the Chamber, and I appreciate you cannot remember or you cannot be asked to use the exact words that Mr. Sacic used, but can you tell the Chamber what Mr. Sacic told Mr. Cermak after they returned from Grubori at that meeting you're referring to here, what was the conversation and what was substance of Mr. Sacic told Mr. Cermak? Use your own language, if -- you don't have to use the exact words.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I will try to explain in my own words. When we were in the area of Knin, Mr. Sacic, as can be seen from the transcript as well, said that based on all the information he said, and based on the things that could be seen, that there was fighting, that there was a clash in that area, and I said something to that effect. Rather, that there was a clash there, fighting in the area. I cannot recall his exact words at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic was the chief of sector. He was our boss. In that room --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and we are running out of time, so please concentrate on what I'm asking you. To whom did Mr. Sacic say that there was a clash?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, if he said that, he did so to Mr. Cermak, who was in the room, as well as to the others who were there. He did not whisper that into Mr. Cermak's ear. He said that out loud.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you had just returned from Grubori, and you had -- at which point you saw Mr. Cermak, Mr. Sacic, Mr. Janic, and you said you walked around Grubori. Based on what you saw in Grubori, did you note any evidence of a clash? I'm not referring to houses burning or people being killed, but was there any -- did you notice any evidence of combat activity in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: When I arrived in the area of Grubori, what I could see could be described as a clash that had taken place. It would be difficult to assess that in any other way. I believe anyone who was in that area at that time could have supposed that there had been a clash.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What -- what is it that you saw that made you -- made you saw -- might indicate a clash? What was it that you saw there? Because your evidence so far is you saw the burning houses, you saw two bodies. What else did you see?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I'm telling you that when one entered the area, one could suppose that there had been combat. The houses were not burned as after a -- after arson, one could see there were bullet holes and that weapons were used, that there was some real fighting. It is difficult to explain the whole thing now, but based on our experience throughout the war, it looked like there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where were bullet holes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: On the walls. One could see the holes on the walls of two or three houses. However, I don't think I would be able to recall any more details than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when -- at the meeting when Mr. Sacic told Mr. Cermak what you say he told, did Mr. Cermak respond to that? Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at your statement of 2004, Mr. Turkalj, and Madam Usher, if I could have your assistance. And if could you look at paragraph 50. At paragraph 50 you say: "I not recall any particular decisions being made, although it was said that the bodies needed to be buried. It was either General Cermak or Zeljko Sacic who said that the bodies should be buried. The question of an investigation was not discussed while I was there." Now, at what stage did the discussion about the disposals of bodies take place; after Mr. Sacic told Mr. Cermak about the -- the clash or before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I made certain corrections to item 50 of the statement, whereby I said that it was not a formal meeting, and that other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Things were discussed --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about a meeting. I didn't even refer to the word "meeting." My question was at what stage did the discussion about the disposal of the bodies take place, after Mr. Sacic talked to Mr. Cermak about a clash or before, in the course of the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: That conversation could have ensued only following the fact that there been a conflict there and that there were dead people, and that sanitation and hygiene measures were required. It could have only taken place after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, your testimony was you were ordered by Mr. Markac to call for reports from Mr. Celic and the special instructors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have document P566, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue that, Mr. Turkalj, you say it could not have been but after the clash was discussed or was subject of the conversation. That's not logic. It could have been before or after, isn't it, you can talk about dead bodies without discussing a clash. So, therefore, I do not see the logic in what you apparently present as the only logic answer. I mean, if you've seen dead bodies, whether they have to be buried or not, you could have discussed that before you have discussed any clash or after you have discussed any clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would ask the witness to remove his headphones, I think I know in the translation where -- it got lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's a translation problem, then could you take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was, "You could not collect the bodies after a clash had occurred, not the fact that there was a discussion about a clash." I think that's where the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then clear, and then we'd like to have an answer to the question, because that -- if that is the result of -- of an incorrect translation, then we should put the question again to the witness and seek his answer. Mr. Turkalj, there may have been a translation issue. Therefore, I would like to put the question again to you. The issue of the bodies to be buried, was that subject of the conversation before or after the clash that would have taken place in Grubori was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated that the conversation took place in a room in Knin, and I believe the Prosecutor put the question that way. It concerned the conversation that took place in that room in Knin. I also said that I could not recall the conversation in detail. It was a general conversation. The gist of this question was whether these bodies had to be buried and hygiene measures taken. Whether that was said only after the fact that Mr. Sacic said there had been clash there, to me, it seems possible, and that's what I wanted to say, that after the conversation there had been a clash, it was said as part of that discussion that sanitation and hygiene measures were required. I don't know whether I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it was possible that it was said after that, but you're not concern. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not certain. I'm not certain about the discussion in that room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, you issued this order to Mr. Celic and the four instructors on the orders of Mr. Markac, isn't it? That's your testimony. My question to you is: When did Mr. Markac order you to call for this report? On the 1st September itself or before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: This order -- actually, this is my order. It was drafted pursuant to Mr. Markac's orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please focus on my question. My question was, when did Mr. Markac order you to call for reports which led to you issuing this order? Was it on 1st September that Mr. Markac told you to call for this report or before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I received a written order from Mr. Markac to ask for reports from the instructors. I think it was either on the 31st of August or the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While we're on this document, I just want to get you to -- do you know that the incident in Grubori is referred to as 26th August, but we know it was on 25th of August. It's a mistake, isn't it, Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it took place on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was that based on this, you were provided with reports by Mr. Celic and three special instructors, and Mr. Drljo did not -- refused to submit a report, and you, in fact, submitted Mr. Celic and -- the other three reports to Mr. Markac with your order dated 20th September. I'm not going to call those documents, Mr. Celic [sic], those are the documents you handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2004. Now my question to you is: Your testimony was that when you visited Grubori, you asked Mr. Celic as to what had happened, and he had told you that he didn't know what happened because he had taken an elderly civilian to safety. So when you received the report from Mr. Celic, which is already now in evidence, where there is reference to combat activity, did you confront him as to the difference or the fact that he is now tendering a written report which was different to what he told you in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I can answer this question by telling you that I did not see any sort of reports. The reports that the members wrote on the ground, they sent to those who were in charge of the action. They were not duty-bound to send them to me. There was the headquarters and the command who received such details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... call the documents so that we don't waste any further time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call P564, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now based on this order of yours, Mr. Celic submitted a type written report to you, which you handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor, which we will see on the screen in a moment. Your testimony, Mr. Celic [sic] according to what you told the members of the Prosecutor is that when you visited Grubori --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Ms. Mahindaratne keeps referring to Mr. Turkalj as Mr. Celic in the transcript, and it's just confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, now your testimony is when you went to Grubori with Mr. Celic and Mr. Balunovic, Mr. Celic told you when you asked him to what happened that he did not know what happened because he had taken an elderly civilian to safety. Now that is your testimony, correct? That is what you have told us. Now, when you received this report from him, did you ever confront him with the fact that in this report he gives details of the events in Grubori, as opposed to previously, when you questioned him, he told you that he did not know what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I will give you my answer again. We can see that the report we have on the screen was sent to the action headquarters and not to me. I only forwarded it further, and the members who took part in the action sent it -- the report to the HQ, and in this way, I met my obligation toward Mr. Markac to furnish the reports by members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Turkalj, that being the commander of the Lucko Unit, when there is a serious matter involved, which is the incident in Grubori, and your subordinate commanders submit reports to you to be forwarded to Mr. Markac, you did not even read them? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I read the reports, though I was not required to, I did read them, and I did what my task as the Lucko commander, I said that a report should be furnished considering the Storm encirclement action, and I forwarded them to Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So beyond -- beyond just forwarding the reports, Mr. Turkalj, as commander of the Lucko Unit, you were not interested in finding out for yourself what the truth was, is it; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the statements from members, and I don't see that this should be in any other way. I cannot change their reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Turkalj, but your testimony was very clear. You said that when you questioned Mr. Celic and then you returned from Grubori and you questioned Mr. Balunovic and the other instructors and many other members of the Lucko Unit, they all told you that they did not know what happened, yet later on, you see these same people submitting written reports which contain information completely different to what they told you. So as a commander of the Lucko Unit, are you saying you did not so much as confront them about this contradiction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are quite a few assumed facts in that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. But the question simply is, based on the information you apparently received the day before from Mr. Celic, after you had read his report, and as you said, you forwarded it, did it never come to your mind that there was an inconsistency that you should discuss with Mr. Celic in order to prevent that the reporting might be untruthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my answer. The reports were sent to the action headquarters, which had to, in turn, report on all the events including this action and including the events in the area of Grubori. I as the unit commander did not have the competence to command the action. I wasn't down there and was not able to know what happened there. The reports I received, I find relevant. As I said, I could not change them in any way, and I forwarded them to Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, may I ask you one additional question then. You received the report. You knew what Mr. Celic had told you before. You read the report. You forward the report. Were you aware that at that moment the version that was told to you was not the same as the one that was put in the written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celic told me that in the conversation with Sacic, he was told to write another report. I stated as much. Mr. Celic also said that he did not have reason to doubt what had happened there, since he himself was not present in Grubori. That was the information I received, and the only other thing I could do was to forward the incoming reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is not an answer to my question. My question was whether you were aware of the difference or inconsistency between what Mr. Celic had told you and what you found in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celic had told me that he was not present in Grubori, when we're talking about that particular event. And he told me that Mr. Sacic explained to him that another report had to be drawn. In this way, I did not check these reports at a later stage. I believe my answer is very clear. I did not double-check this report subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now Mr. Celic told that you Mr. Sacic had told him to write another report, and your testimony is that Mr. Celic told -- that Mr. Sacic had told him what to write. This testimony is it for the record at V000-5305, page 43, page 59, and page 76. Now, did you ever ask Mr. Sacic from where he obtained the information, which he -- based on which he dictated -- or sorry, told Mr. Sacic to write this version of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you referred to Mr. Celic to write a new report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Mr. Sacic on from where he obtained the information regarding the incident, based on which he told Mr. Celic to write the second report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document P625, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, was there a register maintained of all weapons issued to the individual members of the Lucko Unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: Members of the Lucko Unit signed up for their weapons according to the register of issued weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that during the investigation initiated into the events of Grubori in 2001 that a list of weapons issued to members of the Lucko Unit in August 1995 was compiled and submitted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I don't really remember the list. I do know, however, that all the members were issued with weapons and that records were made thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page 8 of both the English translation and the Croatian version. Mr. Turkalj, your name is at number 42. Are the details of the weapons recorded against your name correct, as those that you were in possession of in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe that this sort of weaponry was issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I call up document P578, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Turkalj, your testimony was that you were not aware of any of the weapons of the Lucko Unit being examined for forensic analysis in relation to the events in Grubori. For the record this evidence is at V000-5305, that is section 3, page 136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, 65 ter numbers and ERN numbers are not searchable for anyone who looks at this transcript later, what will remain, exhibit numbers or MFI numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, let me give an exhibit number. P1152, page 136. That is section 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, do you recall this order that was issued to you by Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not yet in the 5.000s, Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please give the right P number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: P1152, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, P1152. I'm sorry, I read something in the 5.000s, but I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to -- my learned colleague to pose a foundation for the -- that document because it's obviously that the document has been issued on -- on the late 1999, and it's obviously out of scope of the indictment. So what will be the foundation for showing up this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an exhibit in evidence, and it relates to disposal of weapons of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for two reasons. First of all, it is it in evidence, Mr. Mikulicic. Apparently, either you have not objected to it, or such an objection was denied. And second, one couldn't say that any document outside the time-frame of the indictment is for that reason irrelevant. We have seen a lot of documents from after 2.000, especially in relation to these events which I never noticed that they were considered to be irrelevant. So, therefore, Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm have to say, Mr. President, I am having trouble to move on fast because you have both counsel from the same Defence party objecting, I recall, in fact, once Chamber did indicate that was not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're right, and could we seek that counsel -- and especially on the last objection. If there's a good reason to assume that one counsel would know far better on certain matters that an objection would be justified, that I would not, under all circumstances, disallow if it is practical, and to force one counsel, first, to consult other, but then, of course, it should be on matters which really make sense. And, Mr. Mikulicic, I regret to say that, that I had to tell that you if a document is in evidence, that relevance, mainly based or exclusively based on time-frame is not an objection which should not be taken very seriously. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, do you recognise this order? This was issued to you by Mr. Markac directing to you send a number of weapons belonging to the Lucko Unit for repair and to be written off. If you wish to see the next page, I can ask that the next page be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: There's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this, in fact, has a list of weapons attached to. I'm not going to waste time we don't have the time to go through a comparison of the list of weapons attached to this document, and the previous list that we looked at which indicates weapons which were in the possession of members of the Lucko Unit in August 1995. But I can tell you there are a number of weapons in both lists which are the same. Now, when you were sent this order, did it ever confer to you or were you concerned, particularity in the context that what happened in Grubori was a still an open matter and there was serious allegations against members of the Lucko Unit, that weapons should have been reserved, weapons used by members of the Lucko Unit in August 1995, should have been preserved instead of being sent for repairs or to be written off and dealt with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a pretty leading question. We're getting here into almost a paragraph worth of question without really giving the witness a chance to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Turkalj, when you received this order, did it ever come to your mind that it may have served the interest of finding the ultimate truth on the Grubori incident to preserve these weapons for investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me first observe that the 1999 order we see here was an usual order, based on the technical examination of weapons plan under which the weapons were regularly sent for checks and repairs. I'm talking about the orderly condition of weapons. Weapons would be sent to the workshop or to -- or were actually checked for their condition within their unit, and the unit -- the commission would be consisting of men from the logistics unit and the technical repairs unit. The weapons found to be malfunctioning would either be sent for repairs or would be written off, or if in good order, they would be sent back to the unit. Back in 1999, when this order arrived, I did not really think about the weapons having been used at any point during the war or who may have been wielding a particular rifle during the war, and I'm not referring specifically to this event but to the war activities in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript, I first wanted the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transcript reads page 91, line 12, "unusual order." I understood it was an usual.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who initiated this move? Did you request Mr. Markac to have the weapons subject to a technical inspection at this stage, or was that initiated by Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was regular procedure and the logistics department within the special police force dealt with this as well as the technical repairs department of the Ministry of the Interior. Let me just add that weapons inspection was standard procedure, regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may have document 2809, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, I want to show you just another document quickly. And if we could go to next page, Mr. Registrar, on the English version. No, I'm sorry, on the same page. Now, this is a follow-up order where -- after the technical inspection and the commission has issued the decision on the weapons to be written off, Mr. Markac has sent this order to you, and at paragraph -- the last paragraph reads: "In this context the commander of the police administration's special police ATJ Lucko is required to issue an order to the logistician regarding deletion of weapons from the record through a decision on write-off weapons and file this decision in the units archives." Now, why was it required to delete -- no, first question, how do you delete the records of weapons from -- or how do you delete the weapons from record? What is the process involved in deletion? Do you discard the issue cards, or how is it done?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP TURKALJ
utterances.text: In relation to this decision on the write off of weapons, this isn't an order really, it is said that an order should be issued to the logistics officer, the person who is in charge of maintaining the records of weapons and of the weapons stored because the procedure was, and is today, that where weapons are written off, they have to be deleted from the records of the weapons in possession of a given unit because they are no longer in the possession of that unit, where a piece of weaponry is written off, it has to be deleted from the records. And this was not just true for weapons but for the materiel and technical equipment in general, and this was the way in which records and statistics were kept within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1156 is admitted into evidence, in the absence of any objections. Mr. Turkalj, I have one additional question in relation to this. These are quite detailed instructions and orders on what you explained to us was a routine matter. Were such orders about -- to the level what weapons for inspection or weapons malfunctioning, apparently Mr. Markac being aware of the malfunctioning of the weapons, was that always dealt with at this level? Would for every weapon that should be inspected or being destroyed, were there always orders signed by Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of its regular procedure the sector of the special police conducted the supervision of units and of the materiel and technical equipment used by its members, in terms of they're being in good order and condition. The condition that I referred to, and I said who it was composed of, if the commission found that the weapons were malfunctioning, they would be written off, or otherwise sent back to the unit. Orders to that effect always came from the sector of the special police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether it was always at the level of Mr. Markac, and whether he always signed such orders, or whether the matter was dealt with at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was mostly at the level of Mr. Markac. That was the usual procedure. The supervision itself came from the sector of the special police, and upon their orders, and when I'm saying the sector of the special police, the chief of that sector was Mr. Markac. That was the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I therefore take it that instructions for inspection or sending back weapons, once repaired, to the units, et cetera, that if you say, Mostly at the level of Mr. Markac, that -- well, let's say, in 80 per cent of the weapons which were dealt with in this system, that you would receive orders, or decisions signed by Mr. Markac himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Decisions of this sort were signed by Mr. Markac. When I mentioned -- well, as far as the level of the sector of the special police, Mr. Sacic, assistant to the sector, could also deliver such decisions. I can't claim whether it was always Mr. Markac or whether it was Mr. Sacic as well. I said that predominantly such decisions came from Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. No, I'm looking at the clock. I should withdraw my invitation, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not yet at your full four hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I was hoping not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're close to it. Would you please consider that over the weekend, that you're close to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Turkalj, we'd like to see you back on Monday, at 9.00 in this same courtroom. And I again instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you are still about to give. In the absence of any procedural matters, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Monday, the 15th of December, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
